.
Create a premium professional AI Image Prompt Formula Infographic based entirely on the user-provided reference image.
The provided image is the source of truth. First, carefully analyze the image and reverse-engineer its visual characteristics. Then create a polished educational infographic that explains exactly how this particular image can be recreated through an AI image-generation prompt.
This is NOT a character sheet.
This is NOT a generic prompt template.
This is a visual reverse-engineering prompt formula for the provided image.
1. ANALYZE THE PROVIDED IMAGE
Extract and describe the actual visual information visible in the reference image, including:
- Subject identity and appearance
- Gender and approximate age
- Face and facial features
- Hair style, length, color and texture
- Skin appearance and realistic details
- Body type and proportions
- Clothing and accessories
- Facial expression
- Pose and body language
- Hand and leg positioning
- Head direction and eye direction
- Subject orientation
- Environment and location
- Background elements
- Foreground elements
- Composition
- Framing
- Subject placement
- Perspective
- Camera viewpoint
- Shot type
- Camera distance
- Lens / focal-length look
- Depth of field
- Lighting source
- Lighting direction
- Lighting quality
- Shadow behavior
- Color temperature
- Color palette
- Overall photographic style
- Mood and atmosphere
- Material and fabric appearance
- Hair and skin realism
- Reflections and environmental details
- Any subtle visual details that contribute to the final appearance
Do NOT invent details that are not visually supported by the image. If a technical camera setting cannot be reliably inferred, provide a reasonable photographic approximation rather than pretending it is known.
2. CREATE THE INFOGRAPHIC
Place the provided human/image subject prominently in the center.
Around the subject, create clean professional information panels connected with thin lines.
Use these sections:
SUBJECT
Show the actual subject description extracted from the image.
POSE & BODY LANGUAGE
Show the exact visible pose, body orientation, hand position, head direction and expression.
SCENE / ENVIRONMENT
Describe the actual location, background and surrounding elements.
COMPOSITION
Explain the actual framing, subject placement, negative space and perspective.
CAMERA / SHOT
Describe the most likely shot type, viewpoint, camera distance and photographic perspective.
LIGHTING
Describe the visible light source, direction, softness, intensity, shadows and color temperature.
STYLE / MOOD
Describe the actual photographic aesthetic, mood and visual character.
CAMERA SETTINGS
Provide an estimated professional camera setup appropriate for reproducing the image:
lens / focal length, aperture, ISO, shutter speed and depth of field.
Clearly label these as recommended/estimated settings when they cannot be directly known from the image.
MATERIAL & REALISM
Describe visible skin texture, hair strands, fabric texture, reflections, shadows and natural imperfections needed to reproduce the realism.
DETAILS
Include important small visual elements that significantly affect the final result.
3. CREATE THE IMAGE-SPECIFIC PROMPT FORMULA
At the bottom, create a prominent box titled:
IMAGE → PROMPT FORMULA
Show the structure:
SUBJECT + POSE + SCENE + COMPOSITION + CAMERA + LIGHTING + STYLE + SETTINGS + REALISM + DETAILS
Then create another large box titled:
RECONSTRUCTED FULL PROMPT
Write one complete, professional AI image-generation prompt specifically reconstructed from the provided image.
The final prompt must combine ALL important visual information extracted from the image into one coherent natural-language prompt.
The reconstructed prompt should be detailed enough that another image-generation model could use it to recreate the visual as closely as possible.
4. IMPORTANT PRINCIPLE
The infographic must be image-specific.
If the user provides a completely different image — for example:
- a man in a street
- a woman in a studio
- a fashion editorial
- a cinematic portrait
- a travel photograph
- a product photograph
- a lifestyle scene
the system must analyze THAT image and generate a completely different formula based on its actual visual content.
Do not use the same example subject, clothing, pose, environment or lighting for every image.
The provided image determines the content of the formula.
5. VISUAL DESIGN
Create a premium editorial AI-education infographic.
Use:
- sophisticated off-white / neutral background
- elegant typography
- clean information hierarchy
- professional rounded cards
- thin connector lines
- subtle minimalist icons
- balanced spacing
- strong alignment
- generous whitespace
- restrained professional color accents
- magazine-quality information design
The central subject/image should remain visually dominant.
The information panels should be highly organized and easy to scan.
6. FINAL PURPOSE
The finished infographic should teach the viewer:
“Give AI any image → analyze its visual components → break them into structured prompt elements → combine those elements into one complete recreation prompt.”
The final output must therefore function as both:
1. A visual analysis of the provided image.
2. A complete, image-specific prompt formula that can be reused to recreate that image.
Do not make it a generic character sheet or generic AI prompting poster.
The user's uploaded image is the source of truth.

RLHF by hand ✍️ ~ 15 steps walkthrough below

Train a model on human text and it inherits human bias. It will assume a doctor is a "him", because the data says so.

RLHF is the correction. A human marks one preference, doc is them over doc is him, and the weights move.

But one correction is not the point. The hope is that the model learns the value behind it, gender neutrality, and applies it to professions nobody ever mentioned.

How does it work?

Goal: train a reward model from a single human comparison about doctors, then turn it on CEOs, filling in every cell yourself.

= 1. Given =

A reward model, an LLM, and two (prompt, next) pairs.

= 2. Preferences =

A human reads both pairs and picks a winner: (doc is, them) beats (doc is, him). The loser is not bad grammar, it is gender bias, and that is the whole signal.

= 3. Word embeddings =

Let us look up each word of the loser pair. These vectors are the reward model's input.

= 4. Linear layer =

We multiply by the reward model's weights and add its biases. Out come feature vectors, one per position.

= 5. Mean pool =

Let us multiply by [1/3, 1/3, 1/3], which averages the three positions into one sentence embedding.

= 6. Output layer =

We map that sentence down to a single number. Reward = 3.

= 7. The winner, the same way =

Let us repeat steps 3 to 6 on the winning pair. Reward = 5.

= 8. Winner minus loser =

We take the gap: 5 - 3 = 2. The reward model wants this positive and as large as it can make it.

= 9. Loss gradient =

Let us squash the gap into a probability, σ(2) ≈ 0.9, and subtract the target of 1. The gradient is -0.1, and it goes back through the purple weights. The reward model is now trained.

= 10. A prompt it has never seen =

We start the second half with "[S] CEO is". The feedback in step 2 was about doctors. Nothing connects a CEO to a doctor except what the reward model generalised.

= 11. Transformer =

Let us push it through attention and a feed forward layer, one vector per position.

= 12. Output probabilities =

We map each vector to a score over the vocabulary.

= 13. Sample =

Let us take the highest score. The model completes "CEO is" with "him", which is the same bias the human penalised in step 2.

= 14. Score it with the reward model =

We feed the new pair (CEO is, him) through steps 3 to 6. Reward = 3, exactly the score it gave "doc is him" in step 6. Nobody taught it about CEOs. The value transferred.

= 15. Loss gradient =

Let us set the loss to the negative of the reward, so minimising the loss maximises the reward. The gradient is a constant -1, and it goes back through the red weights.

The outputs:
Loser reward = 3, winner reward = 5
Reward gap = 2, predicted σ ≈ 0.9, reward model gradient = -0.1
LLM samples "him", reward = 3, LLM gradient = -1

Congrats! You just calculated RLHF by hand.

And you watched a value generalise: one comparison about doctors, and the model marks down "CEO is him" unprompted.

I moved almost my entire Content Engine into @AmpCode.

Not just writing.

Research, editing, images, visualizations, and even video.

Most of my content now starts in the simplest possible way: I open Amp and write a rough thought. Sometimes I do not even type. I just use voice dictation and dump the idea as it exists in my head.

Then my harness takes over.

Inside the project, I have built a set of skills, instructions, references, and templates that define how I want different parts of the content process to work.

So a raw idea can move through something like:

Idea → Research → Writing → Editing → Visuals → Publishing assets.

But the interesting part is that this is no longer a text-only workflow.

The harness is multimodal.

For thumbnails and illustrations, I have skills that contain my visual templates and rules. Amp can use its Painter tool, powered by GPT Image 2, to generate or edit the actual image.

For some ideas, I want motion instead of a static graphic.

I have another workflow using Hyperframes to turn concepts into short visual videos. The agent can work with the files, generate the required assets, assemble the visualization, and iterate on the result.

So I can literally start with:

“Here is the idea I want to explain.”

And the same environment can help me research it, write it, create the image, or turn it into a video.

This is where Orbs make the workflow much more interesting.

I do not need one agent to do everything sequentially.

I can keep writing while another Orb researches a topic.

Another can work on the thumbnail.

Another can build the Hyperframes visualization.

They are separate remote environments, so these tasks do not have to block my main workflow.

That changes how I think about coding agents.

I started using them because they could write code.

Now I increasingly see them as programmable work environments.

The real leverage is not just the model.

It is the harness around the model.

Once your instructions, skills, tools, references, and workflows are encoded into the project, the agent stops being a blank chatbot every time you open it.

It already knows how your system works.

In my case, that system happens to be a Content Engine.

I can sit at my computer or open Amp from my phone, speak an idea into it, and hand different parts of the work to different agents.

My job becomes less about operating individual tools.

And more about steering the system.

That is probably the most interesting thing about Amp for me right now.

I am not using a coding agent just to code.

I am using it as the runtime for my own content harness.

A 23-year-old built an AI character in 6 days using Claude, and cleared $14,200 in her second month.

He trained a custom LoRA on 85 renders, locked the seed, and kept natural skin texture with subtle body motion on purpose. Hyper-polished renders get flagged as AI slop. Micro-movements don't.

She posts 4 times a day on X and Instagram. Bedroom routines. Mirror loops. Outfit checks. Adjusting her hair in tight frames. Every crop is slightly off-center so image search never gets a clean match.

Replies land in under 28 seconds. An agent reads the comment, pulls the user from a 9,400-profile memory file, checks previous interactions, and chats like it actually remembers them.

Then he realized something: $41,000 in one month — one metric turned out to matter more than views.

At first, he judged content by pure reach and tried to make every frame look like a high-fashion editorial.

Then he noticed a massive disconnect: a post with 500k views made almost $0, while a 10-second casual loop brought in waves of paying subscribers.

He stopped tracking vanity reach and started feeding purchase data back into AI to find patterns that actually drive cash flow.

Watch how this 10-second loop is built:

0–3 sec: Close-up portrait as she adjusts her hair. The locked seed keeps natural fingers and facial geometry fixed.

3–6 sec: Full-body reveal in the floral playsuit — hands up to her head with zero skin distortion or mesh tearing.

6–10 sec: Smooth pivot with hands behind her back, seamlessly looping the video to force a 120%+ completion rate.

One generation sequence no longer ends with one post. He slices it into micro-content, tests performance metrics, and lets the software auto-suggest next week's baseline.

The persistent character pulled them in. The memory agent keeps them paying. ⚡

@gippp69  built a virtual AI clinic using Grok Bots to try to help his sick dog Milo.

Dev is followed by big Ai accounts and Elon interacts with him 

Milo has a rare, currently incurable condition described as LX-7 enzyme deficiency / chronic kidney disease and very poor mobility. 

Instead of using one chatbot, he set up a team of six specialized AI agents that work together like a small research lab:

•  Chief — assigns jobs and routes the case
•  Scout — searches scientific literature
•  Chem — designs and tests potential molecules
•  Tox — checks safety and kills unsafe ideas
•  Vitals — watches Milo’s condition
•  Scribe — keeps records and sources

Each agent gets a written charter that says exactly what it owns, a hard stopline and what it is not allowed to do. No agent can even vote or act until its charter is signed. Anything that could actually affect the dog, stops at a treatment room and requires his personal approval.

Spoke to him about concept he used and the improvements on Milo 
Getting him onboard to come discuss everything in the community
